title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
In this analysis, I look at median home values across counties in Maryland, and ask which communities measure most and least reliably. I am interested in seeing which counties are the least reliable in data. I wonder if I can find potential explanations in those discrepancies, if the least reliable counties may tend to respond to the survey less or misrepresent their counties based on MOE.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
As a MD resident, this makes sense that the counties we know the least about/have less accurate information on, are the counties with smaller populations. Somerset county has the highest MOE at 9.1%, I don’t really know anyone from there, nor Kent (5.8%) or Garrett (4.7%) county, the top 2 and 3 for highest MOE. These are counties with wild horses, other wildlife, and beaches. The counties we pass through on our way to Ocean City where you can’t really see houses. Somerset county, MD is one of the few counties in the Northeastern-ish US that only recently needed fiber (internet cable) built to. Basically, not a lot of people live there. Not enough to have a significant statistics on median home value. This is likely because of sampling variability in results we can’t account for in small counties. ACS is a survey of a sample so bigger counties like Baltimore and Montgomery would receive more responses to the survey than a small one like Somerset. There could be a really expensive or really cheap house that could be skewing the data that adds to statistical uncertainty in a small county. For state agencies studying the variable, median home value, smaller counties would be at a disadvantage. For example, if a state agency wants to allocate funding such as decreasing or increasing the construction of affordable housing units or even discounting/increasing APR for homeowner loans, residents of these smaller counties that need funding would be left out since the data likely misrepresented them or left them out completely. For example, Somerset county’s estimated median home value is $164,300, for those looking to move to Somerset county, they wouldn’t receive much assistance as the predicted value is lower than most counties in MD.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text: In the article, “New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty” by Alfred Lubrano for the Philadelphia Media Network, Lubrano reports on the American Community Survey’s 5-year estimate for 2013 to reveal a growing number of white people living in poverty in Philadelphia’s neighborhoods. Fairhill being the prime example, he uses this to describe how white people in the area have struggled to recover from the recession and face addiction. Also, noting that Eastwick faces a higher number of people living in poverty, the article suggested low-income African immigrants are to explain for this change. A number of factors contribute to the poverty crisis in Philadelphia. My report will attempt to evaluate and validate this poverty rate change at the tract-level. I will be analyizing the following variables mentioned in the article; poverty rate(count of people with poverty status;B17001_002 divided by the total population for people with poverty status; B17001_001) and population (B01003_001). I will be using numbers from the 5-year estimate for 2006-2010 and 2013-2017, the same years the article used in comparison to make different points on the change in poverty rates in Philadelphia. As the article does not explicitly define the ACS variables they used, I will continue this report under the assumption that ‘poverty rates’ are the percent of people that fall below poverty level not separated by gender or age.

      cv <= 40 ~ "🟡",

    ),
    flag = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE     ~ "Unreliable"

    NAME = str_remove(NAME, ", Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania")
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(cv)) %>%

get_poverty <- function(yr) {
  get_acs(
    geography = "tract",
    variables = "B07012_002",

    county = "Philadelphia",
    year      = yr,
    survey    = "acs5"
  ) %>%
    mutate(period = paste0(yr - 4, "-", yr))
}

poverty_change <- bind_rows(
  get_poverty(2010),
  get_poverty(2017)
)

poverty_wide <- poverty_change %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, estimate, moe) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from  = period,
    values_from = c(estimate, moe)
  )

# 90% confidence significance test
rate_tested <- tract_2010 %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, rate_2010 = rate, moe_2010 = rate_moe) %>%
  left_join(
    tract_2017 %>% select(GEOID, rate_2017 = rate, moe_2017 = rate_moe),
    by = "GEOID"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    change      = rate_2017 - rate_2010,
    se_1        = moe_2010 / 1.645,
    se_2        = moe_2017 / 1.645,
    se_diff     = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff    = se_diff * 1.645,
    z           = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  )

rate_tested %>% count(significant)

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text:
Part 3
The article makes numerous claims that can and cannot be backed by this replication. 1. The overall claim that poverty across the city has risen in 2013-2017 from 2006-2010 appears to be supported in that the average rate of poverty in the 2013-2017 estimate is truly 26.1% and is higher in comparison to the rate for 2006-2010 at 25.5%. 2. This replication study does not support the article’s claim that poverty rates in 22 majority-white neighborhoods have increased, dramatically in some. This is largely due to the fact that 16% of the tracts (63 out of 384) show statistically significant change with 90% confidence. This study as is does not determine which neighborhoods that number encompasses or if there was a large, dramatic increase in poverty rates. It also does not support the claim that neighborhoods surrounding the Philadelphia International Airport has the highest poverty rate increase of any community, it reveals NA due to lack of populace.
3. We cannot determine in this replication backs any claim about neighborhood poverty rates, race-based poverty rates, or that any other demographic influencing poverty has a statistically significant effect on poverty rates. Doing so would require a different filter on ACS data and include a study on more variables, such as median income, and their significance. We do not know the exact variables they used to determine the proportion of white people in Fairhill and most explanatory variables such as immigration status and employment mentioned in the article were collected through testimony and qualitatively.

  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%

Code
# Merge overlapping polygons so nothing is double-counted
ez  <- layer1 %>% st_make_valid() %>% st_union()
rda <- layer2 %>% st_make_valid() %>% st_union()

# % of each tract's area covered by a polygon layer
pct_in <- function(poly) {
  covered <- st_intersection(select(tracts, GEOID), poly) %>%
    mutate(a = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    group_by(GEOID) %>%
    summarize(a = sum(a))

  a <- covered$a[match(tracts$GEOID, covered$GEOID)]
  replace_na(a, 0) / as.numeric(st_area(tracts)) * 100
}

  mutate(
    pct_ez = pct_in(ez),
    pct_rda = pct_in(rda),

  )

            cv_rmse = cv_rmse(formula, tracts), notes = notes)

log_model("m4", "distance to Redevelopment Area", update(base, . ~ . + pct_ez + pct_rda + dist_rda_mi))

title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 7: Reflection

What helped, and what didn’t? The portion of a tract inside a Redevelopment Area helped most, lowering CV RMSE from 5.56 to 5.21 percentage points of vacancy. These areas are places the city has already flagged for disinvestment, which my ACS variables, which only describe who lives in a tract, couldn’t see. The squared bachelor’s term disappointed me most. It was significant on its own, but CV RMSE rose from 5.156 to 5.172, probably because the Redevelopment Area variables already captured the signal it was picking up. Logging poverty and grouping tracts by Redevelopment Area coverage each moved CV RMSE by less than 0.02, so neither earned a place in the final model.
Read one coefficient twice. For pct_rda, the β̂ reading is that, holding the other predictors constant, each additional percentage point of a tract’s area inside a Redevelopment Area goes with about [0.04] percentage points higher vacancy. The ŷ reading is that a tract with half its area in a Redevelopment Area is predicted to have a vacancy rate about [2] points higher than an otherwise identical tract with none.
What’s still missing? I’d want to measure housing type, such as the share of units in large buildings or built recently, because vacancy in those places can reflect turnover or lease-up rather than disinvestment. Building permits and zoning layers on OpenDataPhilly could supply this. There’s one layer called “Certified for Rental Suitability” on OpenDataPhilly, I could try to run an analysis and see the relationship with the proximity to places with rental suitability.
How much of the remaining error might be uncertainty or statistical noise? Noise explains only part of it. The largest misses, 15 to 20 points, occur in tracts with CVs of roughly 10 to 25%, where the estimate is fairly precise, so those are real model failures. Misses are smallest where CV is around 35 to 60%, and rise only modestly above 90%, where the estimates are least reliable. Since CV falls as the vacancy rate rises, those large misses are probably high-vacancy tracts the model underpredicts. Still, with about half my tracts above 40% CV, some of the 5-point CV RMSE can’t be reduced by any model.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
text: In the article, “New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty” by Alfred Lubrano for the Philadelphia Media Network, Lubrano reports on the American Community Survey’s 5-year estimate for 2013 to reveal a growing number of white people living in poverty in Philadelphia’s neighborhoods. Fairhill being the prime example, he uses this to describe how white people in the area have struggled to recover from the recession and face addiction. Also, noting that Eastwick faces a higher number of people living in poverty, the article suggested low-income African immigrants are to explain for this change. A number of factors contribute to the poverty crisis in Philadelphia. My report will attempt to evaluate and validate this poverty rate change at the tract-level. I will be analyizing the following variables mentioned in the article; poverty rate(count of people with poverty status;B17001_002 divided by the total population for people with poverty status; B17001_001) and population (B01003_001). I will be using numbers from the 5-year estimate for 2006-2010 and 2013-2017, the same years the article used in comparison to make different points on the change in poverty rates in Philadelphia. As the article does not explicitly define the ACS variables they used, I will continue this report under the assumption that ‘poverty rates’ are the percent of people that fall below poverty level not separated by gender or age.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim
section: Part 3: Which claims do I support
text:
Part 3: Which claims do I support
The article makes numerous claims that can and cannot be backed by this replication. 1. The overall claim that poverty across the city has risen in 2013-2017 from 2006-2010 appears to be supported in that the average rate of poverty in the 2013-2017 estimate is truly 26.1% and is higher in comparison to the rate for 2006-2010 at 25.5%. 2. This replication study does not support the article’s claim that poverty rates in 22 majority-white neighborhoods have increased, dramatically in some. This is largely due to the fact that 16% of the tracts (63 out of 384) show statistically significant change with 90% confidence. This study as is does not determine which neighborhoods that number encompasses or if there was a large, dramatic increase in poverty rates. It also does not support the claim that neighborhoods surrounding the Philadelphia International Airport has the highest poverty rate increase of any community, it reveals NA due to lack of populace.
3. We cannot determine in this replication backs any claim about neighborhood poverty rates, race-based poverty rates, or that any other demographic influencing poverty has a statistically significant effect on poverty rates. Doing so would require a different filter on ACS data and include a study on more variables, such as median income, and their significance. We do not know the exact variables they used to determine the proportion of white people in Fairhill and most explanatory variables such as immigration status and employment mentioned in the article were collected through testimony and qualitatively.
